utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the representative of the Portuguese government introduce themselves for the record. MR. DE SERPA SOARES: Good morning, Your Honour. I'm Miguel Soares, the Director General of Legal Affairs in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Portugal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. MS. GROBA GOMES: Good morning, Your Honour. I'm Mafalda Groba Gomes from the Embassy of Portugal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Today we'll continue to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Probably we'll do so for the remainder of the week. Unless there's anything to be raised, we'll continue. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, your Excellency, Mr. Cutileiro. I'd like to thank you for investing this effort to be here. Did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D05532 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones save for the witness's and the accused's be switched off because of the background noise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5532.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it the statement you provided to my team, the one you see on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Excellency, have you read and signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last page, please, in order to be able to identify the signature.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement accurately reflect what you told my team? Are your words recorded appropriately?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask the same questions today in this courtroom, would your answers be essentially the same as provided in the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: They would indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I seek to tender this package under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just two matters for clarification. First as regards 1D604, which was referred to para 24. However, in the notification, it is referred to as 1D694, which I take it to be a typo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And as regards 1D1335, which is being referred to in para 30, it is said to be a letter from Mr. Karadzic to Ambassador Cutileiro, but I think that the case is the other way around. It's a letter -- it seems to be a letter from Ambassador Cutileiro to Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit the Rule 92 ter statement for Ambassador Jose Cutileiro. Shall we give the number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D2968, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And as regards the associated exhibits, they will be admitted and be given numbers in due course by the Registrar. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to read out a brief summary in the English language for the sake of the interpreters to be acquainted with what is going on. [In English] Jose Cutileiro served as a diplomat for the Portuguese Foreign Service since 1974. In February 1992, Lord Carrington, the Chairman of the European Commission's Conference on the former Yugoslavia asked Ambassador Cutileiro to chair talks on future constitutional arrangements for Bosnia and Herzegovina. The talks began on 13th and 14th February 1992 at the Villa Konak in Sarajevo. On 16th to 18th of March, 1992, the fifth round of talks took place in Sarajevo. At the end of those talks, on March the 18th, 1992, the parties agreed to a Statement of Principles. The Statement of Principles provided, inter alia, for a state composed of three constituent units within the existing borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Each constituent unit and the central organs of the BH committed to act with respect for human rights, full religious freedom, and protection of minorities. The Assembly would be composed of two Chambers - a Chamber of Citizens, and a Chamber of Constituent Units. A four-fifths of majority of the Chamber of Constituent Units would be required for certain decisions. A working group was to be established to define the territory of the constituent units. A map was annexed to the agreement which showed the relative majority in each municipality and would be the basis for the working group, subject to apartments. A referendum would be held to confirm these constitutional principles. By agreeing to those principles, Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leaders committed to having religious and ethnic minorities in the areas covered by the Serb constituent units -- unit and to respect the rights of those minorities. The minorities in question were primarily Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats. On 30th, 31st of March, 1992, the sixth and final round of talks took place in Brussels. An annex was added to the Statement of Principles on respect for human and minority rights by the national authorities and those in the constituent units. A European Community Monitoring Mission would be established to investigate and report on any violations. Dr. Karadzic agreed to this annex. Shortly after the parties agreed to the Statement of Principles, Ambassador Cutileiro began hearing that President Izetbegovic was disavowing his agreement in public statement he made to the Bosnian news media. The Bosnian government formally rejected the Statement of Principles in June 1992. During the period after the Statement of Principles was agreed to, the leaders of the Bosnian Serbs wanted further negotiations on the unresolved issues while the Bosnian government leaders dragged their feet. Notes of Ambassador Herbert Okun of a meeting on April 18, 1992, in Lisbon in which Ambassador Cutileiro met with Cyrus Vance indicate that Ambassador Cutileiro said that he had grown to distrust Izetbegovic in spite of his avuncular manner, and that he is tricky and slippery and he lies. Alija Izetbegovic says some things in private and another in public. The notes also indicate that after that meeting they were joined by Portuguese Foreign Minister Pinheiro. During this meeting, Ambassador Okun's notes indicate that Ambassador Cutileiro said that it was absurd to blame the situation in Bosnia exclusively on the Serbs. All sides are to blame. He repeated that Izetbegovic is very untrustworthy. He always goes back on what he agreed to do. Sometimes after the shelling of persons in the bread queue at Vase Miskina Street, Ambassador Cutileiro had the opportunity to speak with the -- a Portuguese army officer, artillery officer, who was stationed in Sarajevo. The officer told Ambassador Cutileiro that he had participated in the investigation of this shelling and was convinced that the shell had come from the area where the Bosnian government had their positions. Ambassador Cutileiro remained in his role as chair of the Bosnian constitutional agreement negotiations until 14th of August, 1992. Ambassador Cutileiro attended a meeting between Lord Carrington and Cyrus Vance and the Bosnian leaders in London on 26 August 1992. During the meeting, Dr. Karadzic expressed his willingness to return territory to the Muslims, and Professor Koljevic said that it was clearly in the interests of the Serbs to return land in exchange for full political autonomy. Dr. Karadzic supported an agreement for the return of all refugees and stated that he had issued instructions to stop his forces from requiring Muslims and Croats to sign paper indicating they were willing to leave and that any such paper would have no validity. Dr. Karadzic also agreed to accept UN monitors at all Serb artillery positions in and around Sarajevo. Ambassador Cutileiro believes that it was a real tragedy that peace was not achieved through the Statement of Principles that he negotiated in March 1992. A comparison of the map annexed to the Statement of Principles of March the 18th, 1992, and the map which is part of the Dayton Agreement of November 1995 shows that after 3.5 years of war, the result was about the same. Countless lives could have been saved. On 16th of February, 1993, Ambassador Cutileiro wrote a commentary published in the "International Herald Tribune" which endorsed the Vance-Owen Plan and noted that President Alija Izetbegovic's reluctance to accept that the real Bosnia is utterly different from the Bosnia of his wishful thinking has contributed as much as have the dreams of Greater Serbia and the Croatian hegemony to the continuation of the war. Ambassador Cutileiro believed this to be true then and believes it to be true now. In a letter to "The Economist" in December 1995, Ambassador Cutileiro wrote: "After several rounds of talks, our principles for future constitutional arrangements for Bosnia and Herzegovina were agreed by all parties - Muslims, Serbs and Croats - in Sarajevo on March 18th, 1992, as basis for future negotiations. These continued, maps and all, until the summer when the Muslims reneged on the agreement. Had they not done so, the Bosnian question might have been settled earlier with less losses of mainly Muslim lives and land. To be fair, President Izetbegovic and his aides were encouraged to scupper the deal and to fight for a unitary Bosnian state by well-meaning outsiders who thought they knew better." Ambassador Cutileiro believed this to be true then and believes it to be true now. [Interpretation] This concludes the brief summary. At this point in time, I have no questions for his Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Ambassador Cutileiro, as you have noted now, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Alan Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning, Your Honours, and to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And good morning, Ambassador Cutileiro.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, let me begin with a couple of quick clarifications. First of all, is it correct that nothing you say in your statement is intended in any way to justify or legitimise any of the crimes that took place during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Not at all. I mean, I -- I -- the statement is a statement of fact. I was asked about my position towards several points. You -- you have listened and you have seen the quotations from Herb Okun's notes. The quotations also from my articles in the "Herald Tribune" and my letter in "The Economist," and I -- what I did when I answered both the counsel for Dr. Karadzic and yourselves from the Prosecution in Brussels, you asked me about how things had gone and I told you how those things had gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Ambassador. Thank you. And just to clarify, it wasn't a suggestion on my part that there was that inference in your statement. It is simply that your name has come up in various contexts during the course of this case as has reference to the negotiations, and on that basis I wanted to clarify what otherwise seemed pretty clear from your statement. So that's why I asked the question. And I'll ask a similar question for the same reason. Do I correctly understand that the agreement in principles was not intended to be a trigger or a signal to any of the parties to take control of or seize territory that they considered to be theirs or wanted to be theirs?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Not at all. The idea was to convince, to try to help the three parties to get on with the job of getting an understanding among themselves and prevent a very horrible war to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood. Thank you. Ambassador, at paragraph 35 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing so, Ambassador, do you have your statement with you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to have a hard copy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have -- if it is needed here. If you can show it to me in the screen. I have copies of that, but I didn't bring them with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thirty-five, yeah. I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You note in that paragraph that had the Muslim side not reneged on the agreement, "the Bosnian question might have been settled earlier, with less loss of mainly Muslim life and land." Now, first of all, this loss of mainly Muslim life and land took place, as you yourself note in the article in "The Economist" that's cited here, after the Bosnian Serbs "went brutally on the offensive." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I didn't write anywhere that anybody had gone brutally on anything. You are not quoting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's call up then very quickly 1D ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Okay. That is not the correct cite. I'll return to that in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me move on and we'll find that in the citation I had in mind. Secondly, I wanted to note the following, and again this maybe something that's clear from your statement, but I just wanted to clarify that: The -- there were actually -- there was actually more than one way in which the war could have been averted, I take it. First of all, as you point out in the article, the Muslim side could have continued to pursue the agreement in principle and the cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what you refer to in the article. And -- that's one way. And secondly, the other way is that the Bosnian Serb side could have accepted the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent and sovereign state. That would be the other way in which war could be averted; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: There might even have been other ways. You didn't mention the Croats. For instance, the Croats might have also their ideas about ways of improving the situation in Bosnia, but we had decided, we the European -- the European Community's conference, as soon as Croatia got its independence, Lord Carrington was convinced that we would have a problem in Bosnia, because Bosnia had the configuration that you know, with three constituent peoples, the Muslims, the Serbs and the Croats. We thought that the Muslims would want -- the government at that time was a coalition government, if you may remember, made of the people that then went into a negotiation with me into fighting on the ground, and that this -- these people and the situation of the country would probably mean that once was -- Croatia was independent, there might be trouble in Bosnia before Bosnia could get her independence. Therefore, Lord Carrington asked me to start talks between the three -- all the parties. I also saw parties from the opposition, but the main parties were those that -- were the coalition government at the time. And the idea was to find a system that would allow the country to be independent with the agreement of the three constituent nations, which is what the constitutional arrangements of Yugoslavia at the time would require.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, let me just say I --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that was an amplification that was not necessarily fully contained your statement, and so I appreciate that very much. As a general matter, I'm going to ask you to do two things --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- because I have very limited time to speak with you today. Number one, bear in mind that it's not necessary to repeat information that you've already provided in the statement that's before the Court. And number two, try as much as you can to simply focus on the particular question asked and determine from any follow-up questions whether any elaboration is needed. I really hesitate to interrupt you, but I just want to make sure we can get through the questions I have during the time I've been allotted.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that the only way of getting an arrangement to Bosnia was to adhere to the -- what had been agreed in March. In that way or in some other way. And if you look at the Dayton Agreement, and if you look at the maps in the Dayton Agreement, you realise, as my letter to "The Economist" shows, that after three years of a lot of tragedies, you didn't move far from what we had foreseen. Bosnia is what it is. It's not another thing. And you -- the Serbs ideally would have preferred that Bosnia didn't become independent. The Croats would have preferred to annex part of Bosnia or to make it some kind of -- and the Muslims, in particular President Izetbegovic and his people, thought that they could have a unitary state. So the -- if you look at the agreement of March 1992 and you look at the Dayton Agreement slate, well, I was there and I didn't think that we could go into other thing -- Martti Ahtisaari who followed me --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- I really have to try to move forward.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I know you have a wealth of information and ideally we would have as much time as necessary to hear all of your observations about what took place, but if you will permit me to please focus on certain areas given the time constraints I have. First of all, we will be looking at the Dayton map and the map affixed to the Statement of Principles. Before we do, I want to return to what I had asked you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could call up 1D5129.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I had asked you whether the loss of Muslim -- mainly Muslim life took place after the Bosnian Serbs "went brutally on the offensive," quoting an article by you, I think you're correct, I didn't point you to the article reference --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- there. But in this case I'm pointing to the article by you in the "International Herald Tribune." And if we could -- I'm just looking at the bottom of the first column that states the Serbs -- it talks about the aftermath of March 18th, and it states: "The Serbs felt confirmed in their paranoid view of history and went brutally on the offensive."

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Hmm. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Ambassador, you provided us an eloquent explanation just a moment ago about your role as negotiator and facilitator rather than someone who was attempting to impose his own predetermined solution. Your statement refers to a letter from Dr. Karadzic, dated the 5th of June. That's in paragraph 28 of your statement, and that letter has been admitted into evidence as associated with your statement. In addition to the portions of the letter that are reflected in your statement in paragraph 28, the letter goes on to note that the Serbian people feel cheated. And in the letter, Dr. Karadzic states to you that: "If you cannot keep your promises publicly announced and confirmed by the EC," that is the European Community, "we have to protect Serbian people on their ethnic territories." Now, there -- you sent a response to that letter. That was -- that is not referenced in the statement. That's found at P952, and that was on June 12th. And I'll call it up quickly to remind you of that, Mr. Ambassador. And in that letter, you state to Dr. Karadzic that the EC has not made any promises to you. You explain that there were talks on the future constitutional arrangements. You go on to note the agreement on principles, and you further state: "The validity of that agreement, however, can only be upheld if orders and competencies of the constituent units be defined by negotiated consensus and not by force" --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- "and if 'ethnically cleansed' territories are -- be restored to their antebellum ethnical compositions."

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was the letter you sent in --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- response to the June 5th letter referenced in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I think you've referred to this both in your statement and in your remarks thus far, but it's correct that the agreement in principles, that is the agreement that was reached on March 18, 1992, was essentially a preliminary step toward further negotiations and -- and not a final agreement on the resolution of the --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It's written at the end of the agreement. It says that it's the basis for further negotiations or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership emphasised to their followers that it was indeed not a final agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I suppose they did, yes. And that was what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So on the very date of the agreement itself, on March 18th, there was a Bosnian -- a session of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the RS Assembly, at which Dr. Karadzic stated: "We have entered into this process with our strategic goals, and we are accomplishing them stage by stage. We would never have signed this paper as a document, never, never, never." So I just wanted to ask you -- and that's found at D90, at page 43, e-court page 43. I just want to know if you were aware of the emphasis that the Bosnian Serb leadership and Dr. Karadzic were placing on the fact that this was not a final agreement.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: No, I was not. What I was aware of was that during -- at different stages of our negotiations, Dr. Karadzic told me that he had to get agreement from his -- what he called his Assemblies, the Serbian Parliamentary Assembly, to agree or not agree to some points even before we reached the Statement of Principles. And -- and then he went, and he usually got that agreement, and I think -- that's what I know. That, I mean, he was representing a group that was the Assembly of the Serbs, and he had to see with them whether what he had proposed to them was accepted by them or not. I suppose it -- all sides would have had their difficulties with -- with their own people, but I was not a member of that Serbian Assembly, as you can imagine, so I don't know exactly what went on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mr. Ambassador, that Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership were emphasising their satisfaction with the agreement in principle because it meant the end of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me read you a couple of things that were said in that regard by Dr. Karadzic and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership. For example, in an interview that we'll have an opportunity to see a bit later, Dr. Karadzic said the map was not acceptable, but for the first time this was about the separation of Bosnia into three pieces. That's 65 ter 45284. At the 39th Assembly session in 1994, Dr. Karadzic said about the Cutileiro process: "We pulled them into that at that time when they said we accepted the division in three and that it would be based on ethnicity. At that moment, Bosnia was finished for the international community. That was a great achievement. We were happy when they rejected the maps." At the 42nd Assembly session -- and that is, for the parties' reference, P1388. At the 42nd Assembly session, that's P1394, this is at pages 81 and 81, Dr. Karadzic said: "We won it on 18 March thanks to Mr. Krajisnik's skills. That was the first time that Alija said yes to three Bosnias on ethnic basis and that was fatal for him. That was the moment when Bosnia collapsed and we were accepted as a party in the conflict. If they had ignored us, kept silent and acknowledged Bosnia and then afterwards said that some rebels were overthrowing their own state, we would have faced difficult problems. Nobody would have talked to us." And again Dr. Karadzic, this time at the 37th Assembly session at P1385, pages 114 through 115: "This will be the first time in history that a country is torn apart after the recognition and that the international community accepts it." Ambassador, I take it that you were not aware of these various pronouncements of Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: No, I was not, and the first of them that you read now is from 1994. I had left -- I stopped dealing directly with Bosnia in the summer of 1992. I still attended some meetings of the next conference, the Vance-Owen conference. But you -- okay. I just heard what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the destruction of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state was not consistent with the agreement in principles, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: You cannot take bits of political discourse during some kind of meeting of an Assembly from one side or the other and present them. When I see that, I'm not surprised by that. I think the three sides had a discourse that was complicated with their own basis, if you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect, Ambassador --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- I asked you earlier to please focus on my questions because of my limited time.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes. Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I'm simply asking you whether or not the destruction of Bosnia was considered to be part of the agreement in principles?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: The agreement in principle was made to keep -- you see, if I may again disturb you a bit with my going off the point, but it's very short. It's very short. The Europeans, basically, wanted Bosnia to go on. We didn't want any change of the internal borders of Yugoslavia. The Croats and the Serbs were not interested in keeping Bosnia. The Muslims were, and that was it. And the agreement, the agreement, was a way of trying to solve that problem. And if I go back to Dayton, that seems to be the viable agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We're going to be -- as I said to you, we'll be looking at the map. Did Dr. Karadzic and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership tell you that they considered that if they could not get what they wanted from negotiations, they would go to more traditional approaches such as the use of force?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: The use of force was taking place already with each side blaming the other at the very beginning, and -- and nobody -- what Dr. Karadzic told me sometimes is that if we didn't manage to get an agreement, there would be a terrible war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just citing one remark from the 11th session of the Assembly, again on March 18th, the quote is, and this is by Mr. Krajisnik, a participant in the discussion, and as you are aware, a close confidant of Dr. Karadzic: "Did we not say that nothing was agreed as yet, that this was working material? Our work is not yet finished, gentlemen. This is just one phase. If we cannot achieve our goal and carry out the mandate we've received from this Assembly, then we will do whatever is necessary to protect our interest." That's D90 at e-court page 34. And I take it that that was consistent with what you just told us you were hearing from Dr. Karadzic and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership about what would happen if the Bosnian Serbs didn't realise the agreement they were seeking.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It was not put to me like that. It was put to me as if we did not go on negotiating on the basis that we had agreed on in March, things would deteriorate into war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now -- now, on February 25th, during the course of the negotiations, Mr. Krajisnik also said the following. That's found at D88. He said: "As a participant in the Lisbon talks, I'd like to add a few remarks." Then he went on: "Gentlemen, we have two options, one to fight by political means to make the most of the present time as a first phase, or to break off the talks and go for what we have done over the centuries, win our own territories by force." And then he continued: "We have the opportunity to preserve the Serbian people in a single state, to preserve the entire Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and have it become part of the Serbian empire." And that's at pages 62 through 63 of D88. Did the agreement in principle, Ambassador, envision that the Bosnian Serb entity would become part of the Serbian empire, that is that the --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Look, what Mr. Krajisnik said, it's a lot of rubbish. I mean, it doesn't make any sense. Perhaps it did to his public at the time, but that was one of the many nonsenses that we had to cope with. The idea was to introduce some kind of common-sense rationality into all that business. That's what the agreement is for. What they said in their Assembly, I wasn't there. I didn't hear him. I'm not surprised, but I'm not shocked either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The short answer, I take it, Ambassador, is that in fact the desire to or objective to unify the Bosnian Serb entity with Serbia and Montenegro was not envisioned by the Statement of Principles?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: On the contrary. It's clear. I suppose it is said somewhere in Statement of Principle that they shouldn't try to -- neither Croats nor Serbs should try to get into either Croatia or Serbia. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we've heard reference to the issue of territory, both in that article in the "International Herald Tribune" we looked to and in various other references here. I take it that it was clear at that time that the issue of what territory would be encompassed by the entities involved was going to be a source of major dispute and major tension; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes. More than that, it was going to be the object of the work -- of a working group that would be set with the help of members of the European Community, as we then were, to try to define precisely the borders of these three constituent units which need not be contiguous, and -- but that work was never done, because meanwhile, things started -- parties start, particularly I think the Muslims but also the Croats, going, at least in what they told me, against the agreement. That is -- to answer your question, it -- obviously there was a lot of work to be done to get the precise limitations of those three constituent units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Dr. Karadzic immediately upon the Statement of Principles was stating the following, and that was on -- again at the 11th session: "We have achieved the quality. This is what Europe recognises. Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina exists. The only remaining question is one of quantity, and it will happen according to our political will, our right to self-determination and organisation. It will happen according to the actual conditions which are up to you," to the -- to his followers, "which are up to you to create."

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes, and so --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So are you aware at the time of Dr. Karadzic's interest in the quantity of the land that --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: The three of them were interested in the quantity of the land. It's obvious if you are going to divide land, if you have a plot and divide it with someone, you have to know exactly the quantity you have to have. This was, of course, one of the complicated things. The problem was not easy, and at that stage they all looked into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you consider, as Dr. Karadzic told his followers, that that would be up to the actual conditions which the people on the ground would be able to create?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I don't know what he meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the map that was affixed to the Statement of Principles was a map, as explained in your statement, that reflected the absolute and relative majorities in the municipalities across Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during the course of the discussions, as Dr. Karadzic and the other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership explained the kinds of transformation or "transformation" of Bosnia they had in mind, various members of the international community advised them that the map of Bosnia does not speak in favour of that kind of division. So, for example, at D1284, those are the notes taken by Dr. Karadzic's chef de cabinet at the time of the discussions. Lord Carrington said specifically at page 3 the map of Bosnia and Herzegovina does not speak in favour of the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And at page 9 of those same notes, as the Bosnian Serb leadership continued to press for ethnic division, Mr. Darwin told them that "I cannot accept that they've been ethnically clean entities because it is not feasible in the field."

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Certainly. Neither Henry Darwin or myself would have accepted ethnical cleansing to -- either by Serbs or, for that matter, by Croats or by whoever. The idea was that this will not be done, and to us in the conference, I think it was Dr. Karadzic himself who agreed that if we came to a final solution of that, there would be -- people would be -- that would have been thrown out from their places would come back to those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'll get --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: We never foresaw, as you can imagine, ethnical cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'll be talking with you about that portion of your statement in a moment too. I'd like to look now at a couple of clips from an interview by Dr. Karadzic in which he talks about why the Bosnian Serb leadership accepted the statement in principles and some of his objections to the existing map of the absolute and relative majorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Those clips are 65 ter 45284A and B.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We're not getting any sound on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was just about to do that, Mr. President. Both in the interest of time and because the -- could we stop that, please. Let's call up the transcript for 65 ter 45284.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For both logistical technical reasons, Ambassador, and in the interests of time, I'm going to show you the transcript of that interview and direct your attention to certain relevant portions. On that occasion, standing before those maps --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: And that was when? Can you refresh my ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We don't have a precise date for it but it would have been after Vance-Owen. So it appears to have been sometime in probably late 1993, 1994, but there's no specific date listed for that. Dr. Karadzic said, as you saw him: "Here before us is the Cutileiro's preliminary map," et cetera. He went on to say: "We accepted the logic of the map and that's why we accepted it because for the first time it was about the separation of Bosnia into three pieces." That's found at page 1, beginning at line 10. And then he goes on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let us collapse the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And he goes on to make the following references in that first paragraph and in the one that follows that. He notes that they acknowledge that there were some Muslims at the foothills of Mount Grmic and Mount Kozara, but they expected they would trade it for something. "Like they expected us to trade something." He indicates down in the next paragraph, again noting that they didn't accept the map: "We weren't satisfied with Eastern Bosnia, with Sarajevo 2. We weren't satisfied with the Neretva River." And if we go to page 2, he again refers to a portion of the map and this time referring, as we see in context here, to north-west Bosnia: "In that regard you can understand now why a green -- a green stain has appeared here." And he talks about Sanski Most and again about Krupa and again about Mount Grmic and Mount Kozara, which is the in the area of Prijedor. Now, Ambassador, first of all, were you aware of the -- some of the specific objections that Dr. Karadzic and/or other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership had to the map that was the working map for the Statement of Principles?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: The map for the Statement of Principles was a preliminary map, so much so, as I told you a minute ago, we had decided to create a working group that was never created. European countries didn't provide on time the people who would help and so on, and it was obvious that the three parties would have objections to bits here or there. So I -- it's perfectly normal. But all this that you have shown to me is in 1993 or 1994, well after the end. We're talking of the -- the preliminary map was an attempt to get the very little goodwill that existed among the parties, to put them together and try to build a viable thing out of that, but any line there was by definition not final, because we had to negotiate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's -- that's understood, Ambassador. I just wanted to know -- you referred to the objections to bits here and there. I just wanted to know if you were aware at the time of Dr. Karadzic's objections to the bit in Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Not that I recall, but it was 20 years ago. I -- maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender 65 ter 45284, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your only question was about -- his objection to Eastern Bosnia with respect to this clip?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder what question did you ask to the Ambassador at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The whole -- the whole thrust of these questions was what were the objections to the map. Then I asked him about specific things, a specific thing that Dr. Karadzic had said about the map. These are Dr. Karadzic's words regarding that very issue, Mr. President. I think it goes directly to the question of what -- what specific concerns were held by the Bosnian Serb leadership and about -- and what specific territory they were -- they sought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Given the position of the Defence, we'll --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6134, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, do you know what steps had been taken prior to the agreement in principle by the Bosnian Serbs to begin the process of ethnic separation? And I include in that such things as the establishment of the Council of Ministers, meetings to discuss the -- ensuring that Serbian power was felt in certain territories, steps towards dividing the police, and so on. Were you aware of that as those discussions were progressing?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Not directly at all. We were -- we had several rounds of conversations with the three parties, what -- each of the parties then with their own. I was not there and I got only indirect information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know that on the very date of the Statement of Principles, March 18th, that steps were -- that the Bosnian Serb leadership, that is, at the Bosnian Serb Assembly, immediately suggested that steps be taken toward implementing ethnic division on the ground, that is, toward asserting physical control over the areas sought?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know the various ways in which the Bosnian Serb leadership defined what they considered to be Serbian territory?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For example, did you know that they considered areas where the Serbs had been a majority before World War II should be Serbian irrespective of which ethnic group was the majority in that area now?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Taken out of context. All that's affirmations of a very nonsensical nature, but we were in Bosnia. The three groups had their own historical memories that were sometimes were very peculiar to an outsider, and everybody was trying to scramble to get what he could from this. So I wouldn't -- I'm not surprised from -- by what I'm hearing, but I don't think that if there had been a strong political will from the top to -- to get this thing through, we might have gotten it through. By the way, in Dayton, if I may go back to that, in Dayton with different perhaps details, certainly many details are different, but we -- we got to that -- the point -- the basic point of this story is: Could we have a unitary Bosnia or did we have to have a tripartite Bosnia? My conviction in the end, during the time I was there, is that only a tripartite thing would work, and that was also the conviction of Dick Holbrooke in the end. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You refer to those as affirmations of a very nonsensical nature. I take it then that --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm referring to the position that the Bosnian Serb entity, that Republika Srpska territory should encompass those areas where the Serbs were a majority prior to World War II. I take it, then, you were not aware that this position was reflected in the declaration of the proclamation of the state on January 9th, 1992, by the Bosnian Serbs, and are not aware that it was actually reflected in the constitution of the Bosnian Serb Republic?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It's possible, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, you referred several times to the map that was affixed to the Statement of Principles and to the -- and that's 65 ter 19151, which is attached to P782, and the map which is part of the Dayton Agreement, which is 1D5129, and you've stated several times that the result was about the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 65 ter 24616. This is a map that combines the two by overlaying the Dayton map on the map affixed to the Statement of Principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the black line represents the Dayton line.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I have difficulty seeing the black -- oh, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I referred earlier to both Mount Grmic and Mount Kozara. I told you that Mount Kozara, where that -- where that was, and the reference we saw in Dr. Karadzic's interview to his objections concerning Sanski Most, and in particular we looked at his objections to the Cutileiro map, that is the map affixed to this statement in principles, relating to Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we look at 65 ter 24616, we see the following municipalities that were once Muslim majority areas and that were identified as such in the map affixed to the Statement of Principles that now fall within the province of the Bosnian Serbs after the -- as a result -- or after the 3.5 years of conflict, and that includes Zvornik, and Bratunac, and Vlasenica, and Srebrenica, and Rogatica, and Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So those are municipalities whose -- the control of which shifted after the conflict began and as a result of the conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Probably, yes, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as this Court is aware, we've seen evidence from the 53rd Assembly by Dr. Karadzic explaining why those areas fell within the province of the Bosnian Serbs, and he said in a quote by now well-known by the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we hear the date for the Ambassador to know to which time this relates?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is what Dr. Karadzic said in -- at the 53rd Assembly session in 1995, and essentially Dr. Karadzic said, Don't let this get around, but there were municipalities where the Serbs were the minority. He referred to the ratios of 30 per cent to 70 per cent. But that the Serbs had to have them for strategic reasons and no one practically is questioning that now.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't there, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 32, as you've explained before, Dr. Karadzic expressed a willingness to return territory to the Muslims. The quote in your statement is: During the meeting of August 26, 1992, "Dr. Karadzic expressed his willingness to return territory to the Muslims ..." Now, the fact is, Ambassador, that Dr. Karadzic didn't say he would return all the territory taken, did he? What he said was -- well, do you remember that? Do you remember that he didn't -- whether or not he said --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I remember exact -- it's in the text. There is a letter, I think, in which that is said, and so what are you trying to ask me? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your statement says he was willing to return territory.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to clarify that he didn't express any commitment to return all of the territory that was conquered or liberated or taken by Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: He didn't say -- he said "territory." He didn't say "all the territory." He didn't exclude it either. The way it was said, the implication of that was, I think, that as we would negotiate, we would come to agreements on different points. But no, he didn't say that he would return all the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He said it was difficult to assess which areas could be handed back and that the precise amount of land that may be returned had not been decided; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Probably, if you have it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's found at 1D5127, which I think came in as an associated exhibit. Now, paragraph 32 also states that, and you mentioned this earlier in your testimony, that Dr. Karadzic supported an agreement for the return of all refugees and stated that he had issued instructions to stop his forces from requiring Muslims and Croats to sign papers indicated -- indicating that they were "willing" to leave.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to the return of people who had fled, there would essentially be, I take it, two extremes on that end of the spectrum. On the one hand, an insistence that everything -- everybody be returned and everything be returned to the status quo ante, and on the other hand -- that is everybody has to come back, and on the other hand, an insistence that the changes resulting from the war, the demographic changes that resulted would have to remain as is. Those would essentially be the two extremes.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: I suppose so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, with that in mind, I'd like to look at some of the positions taken by Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership with respect to that issue and -- and ask if you were aware of those. First of all, let me ask you more generally: Were you aware that from an early stage, even preceding the conflict to throughout the conflict and toward -- to the conclusion of the conflict, that Dr. Karadzic insisted that the factual situation that could be or had been created would be decisive and would be a point that the Bosnian Serbs would insist on?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: That was not phrased to me at all like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you if you're familiar with any of these quotes and then ask you a question about that, because this Court has received extensive evidence that Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership insisted on the enforcement of the factual situation as -- as a means of resolving the conflict and deciding who got what territory. So as early as October 19th --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have a correct cite for this. Just one moment. Okay. As early as December 9th, 1991, Dr. Karadzic was stating: "Europe accepts legality when it does not -- it does not accept legality but the factual status. Therefore we have to be wise enough and prepare both the legality and the factual status." During the course of the war, as we see from -- and that was -- I didn't make it -- I'll get the cite for that in the moment. It's P2554, page 78, and P1479, at page 22, Dr. Karadzic stated in August of 1992: "The European Community will accept the factual situation, which is why we must not make any concessions militarily."

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: He said that to whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: To Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. In --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, Mr. President. If this is a question of whether Mr. Cutileiro heard about these things, how would he have heard about something that Dr. Karadzic said to Mladic. This appears to be an exercise in asking rhetorical questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Hardly. The Defence has proffered this statement for the purpose of advancing certain propositions inferentially and sometimes directly. I'm now going to juxtapose what Dr. Karadzic was saying to other people throughout the course of the conflict and ask the Ambassador -- and I have throughout this examination juxtaposed the things Dr. Karadzic was saying outside the negotiations and sometimes actually in the negotiations with the positions he took in the negotiations and represented were commitments he was willing to make at various times while he was saying other things to his subordinates and followers. I think that's entirely fair and illuminating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course while it is fair, but in order to get the answer correctly, you need to put the quotes in a way so that Ambassador could understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. President, I'm sorry if I wasn't clear, but I thought I indicated I wanted to just identify a few quotes and then put the general proposition rather than doing them one at a time. I thought that made more sense since they form a kind of critical mass --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we pause just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are we still pausing, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: French translation has only now been completed. That's the speed we should proceed. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If I could just come back to this for one moment. The question was, "Let me ask you if you're familiar with any of these quotes," and then he asked him, among other things, of -- he quotes the Mladic diary and asks him about something that Dr. Karadzic said to General Mladic. I don't see how that could be asked in good faith to a witness about what -- was said between Karadzic and Mladic. So it seems like this is just a pretext for putting before the Chamber, as we would do in a closing submission, material and then bouncing off the witness whatever the answer. So I don't think that that's a proper technique, and I think if Mr. Tieger's going to do that, he should at least break it down so that we know the cite that he's taking is actually something that the witness might possibly have been expected to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a -- I think the point has been made. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I'm going to -- Mr. Robinson rises because I think this -- well, I'm not going to rise to his bait.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'm going to read you one more quote in connection with the insistence on the application of the factual situation and that's in connection with the question of whether or not there was a genuine commitment to refugees returning. Okay. At the 46th session Dr. Karadzic said, and that's in 1994: "Our goal is to create a state. How big it will be, we do not know but it has to be in one piece and in order for the state to exist it has to be in one piece. We have to maintain -- maintain this reality as long as the world accepts this idea. We have created new realities." And then he goes on to speak about Zvornik which is won 60/40 in favour of the Muslims but now is populated by Serbs. And he goes on to say: We request Zvornik based on the right which comes out of the new reality. This war had created the new reality." And he continues and concludes: If you want to give Zvornik to the Muslims, then you have to wage a new war in which -- in order to expel these Serbs back to Zenica, we request Zvornik according to this right."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Kindly slow down when reading and pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Did Dr. Karadzic indicate to you in August of 1992, the time when you're referring to his position to you on the return of refugees, that he would be insisting on the implementation and enforcement of the de facto situation that had been created by the war?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One question about the property relinquishment document, that is the -- you stated that Dr. Karadzic said that he had issued instructions to stop his forces from requiring Muslims and Croats to sign papers indicating that they were willing to leave --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I think that is in a letter of his attached. It's not part of my statement as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's actually -- it's actually in paragraph 32 of your statement, Ambassador --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It says --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- if you want to look at that.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, is the Registry calling up -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's the last sentence on that page, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I take it that the international community did not itself accept the validity of that kind of document under the circumstances of the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Papers indicating -- papers requiring Muslims and Croats --

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Those documents were not worth the paper they were written on; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: They might be in the place where they were written and by the people passed them between them, but not to us, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could let Ambassador Cutileiro go if I am able to finish before the break. To that end, I'd like to have P05174 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing so, yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just note I didn't tender 65 ter 24616, the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Overlapping maps. Yes, Mr. Robinson. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6135, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long do you expect, Mr. Karadzic? I'm wondering whether we should take a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not long. Until the break, maybe a minute or two over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed then. Is it okay, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's my first day here, so I'm fresh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Obrigado.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have this map, then, which is P6735.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, what is the position of Serb territories vis-a-vis your map and the Dayton map? I'm trying to say this: The Muslims were left without some parts of their territory, but the Serbs were left without some too. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the political speech in front of the Assembly -- well, do you suppose I had to justify the loss of purely ethnic municipalities such as Drvar, Glamoc, Grahovo -- very well. I withdraw that. I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have D1754. D01754.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, you were asked about whether it was true that I said that I had ordered my forces to stop asking for certain paperwork.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show item 3 to the Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "That forced transfer of people and other illegal measures ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not trying to stop Dr. Karadzic from pursuing this, but I just want to clarify that cross-examination did not ask whether it was true that he said it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the date for the witness's sake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. How is this in keeping with what you stated of me informing you of having issued such an order?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose -- it's here. At least this is the English translation, so I believe it's an accurate translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have D220 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, do you recall a platform of mine I presented on the 22nd of April, 1992, whereby I described my vision of solution to the crisis which I sent to the European Union, the European Community? Please have a look at item 5 where I stipulate our position on what you were asked about during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yes, I read it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How is this in keeping with your understanding of my position during the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: It fits. I mean, what you told me is what is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Excellency. The last document, P5745. [In English] 5745. [Interpretation] Your Excellency, this was a private telephone conversation that was intercepted. You were not privy to it, but I would like you to take a look at page 3 to see what it is that I said privately. You were read out a quote from my Assembly address, and now please have a look at my reply, the fifth item from the stop, beginning with "I, however, accepted." It is a conversation between myself and a Krajina official on -- which date? Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 25th of February, 1992. What am I talking about with this official, because he was in charge of explaining our position to the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic repeat the quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "I, however, accepted that in its existing borders, Bosnia cannot be integral, but in its existing borders this means that we won't join a single part to either Serbia or Croatia." [Interpretation] Your Excellency, how do you interpret this? Is this consistent with the aims of the conference that you were still at the helm of at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSE CUTILEIRO
utterances.text: That is actually touches that one fundamental aspect of the conference itself. The point of the conference was to give as much autonomy as possible to the Serbs and the Croats in the majority Muslim state without, without, infringing the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The understanding of that was sometimes difficult, particularly the understanding of what it meant to be an autonomous part of -- kind of tripartite arrangement. But as for the -- the transcription here of your telephone conversation, yes, that is coherent with -- with what we did at the conference. And as I said, in the beginning, it was one of the points of the conference was to keep the borders. If we -- if not, it wouldn't make sense. It wouldn't even be called -- the thing would not be called principles for the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, thank you very much for coming to testify. I just want to say that even though you were -- even though you were not soft to the Serbs in the least, we did admire your skill and your persistence to preserve peace. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I've been trying to find this document, and -- okay. If you give me just a moment. It was mis-cited, so I just wanted -- before we excuse the Ambassador, I could just take one quick look at the document which I was not able to call up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can look -- I mean, it is in evidence. I can look at it. I won't hold up the Ambassador or the Court any longer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your testimony, Ambassador Cutileiro. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. My thanks also go to the representatives of Portugal, Mr. De Serpa and Ms. Groba. Now you are free to go. Please have a safe journey back home. We will rise all together. We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.05.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stanic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, do you hear me in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the International Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the accused, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you may say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will -- your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in such a case the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am aware of these procedures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stanic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Dr. Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Good day. Good day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I can ask you to pause between my questions and your answers, and can we ask both of us to speak out our sentences slowly so that they can be interpreted to all the parties and so that they can be completely recorded in the transcript. Dr. Stanic, did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can I ask you, please, to look at 1D7232 in e-court, please. Do you see the statement in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We need to make longer breaks. Did you read the statement, and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness the last page, please, so that he can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stanic, is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And since you read and signed the statement, do you believe that the statement accurately reflects what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my statement in its entirety, the way I gave it to the Defence, and it's a statement I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you in the courtroom that the Defence team put to you then, would your answers in essence be the same as those in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I would like to tender this bundle pursuant to 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, I take it you are tendering only two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. We're asking for permission to add them to our 65 ter list as they weren't in our possession at the time when the list was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I would only note that 1D25422 is P05399.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, then. You are tendering only one document. Yes, we'll admit them, and let us give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 92 ter statement will be Exhibit D2982, and 65 ter number 1D06050 will be Exhibit D2983.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to read the summary of Dr. Stanic's statement in English, and then after that, I would ask him about two documents that we received from him. [In English] Dr. Milenko Stanic, born on March the 10th, 1962, in Grabovica village, Vlasenica municipality. He completed his primary schooling in the area of Vlasenica, his secondary schooling in Vlasenica, and graduated from the Economic Faculty in Brcko. He completed his masters in Sarajevo and obtained his doctorate in Banja Luka. He started working in the Vlasenica Boksit mine in 1986 and worked there until the beginning of 1991, when he was elected president of the Vlasenica municipality. At the beginning of 1993, he transferred to the government of the Republika Srpska in the position of Minister of Trade and Tourism. He left the government to become Director of Customs and was a professional deputy in the Assembly of Republika Srpska for one year. Dr. Milenko Stanic did not consider there to be any inter-ethnic problems in any part of the Vlasenica municipality until the formation of the multi-party system, which was then the -- which was then the intolerance began -- which when -- when the intolerance began. Many Serbs were against the break-up of Yugoslavia while the Muslims and Croats were in favour of it, which caused the tensions. At the multi-party elections, the SDA and SDS won an equal number of seats in the Assembly of Vlasenica. In the beginning, the authorities functioned with great difficulty due to the disagreements over key issues. The Muslim representatives attempted to bring down the established constitutional order, whereas Serbs wished to preserve it. Milenko Stanic considered that many of the moves made by the Muslims were unconstitutional, and they used the pressure of mass gatherings in their -- of their supporters in order to implement this unconstitutional attitudes. Muslims stopped fulfilling their military service for the JNA, and during this period the SDA Muslim party were also arming the Muslim population and creating paramilitary formations. Further, Alija Delimustafic, minister of interior, asked police station in Muslim majority municipalities to compile a list of young men who were eligible for military training so that they could be sent to Croatia for training. In the second half of 1991, the SDA gathered and prevented the Tuzla Territorial Defence representatives from requisition -- requisitioning military documentation. The SDA forced its way into the municipal building and very aggressively prevented the files from being requisitioned. A similar incident occurred in -- on 8th of July, 1991, when a large group of Muslims demanded that Dr. Milenko Stanic provide buses for them so that they could collect Muslim soldiers who had been mobilised into the Territorial Defence Vlasenica unit. When the buses arrived, the Muslims asked their fellow nationals to abandon the unit and go home, which almost all of them did, without returning their military equipment. Although the Vlasenica municipality did not give its approval for activities regarding the referendum of B and H to be conducted, certain Muslim members inside the municipal government nonetheless became involved. Once it became clear that the Muslims were seriously engaged in these activities, the Serbs proposed that there should be an official decision that Vlasenica continued to exist within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Tensions and distrust grew amongst both the Serbs and Muslims. To find a solution, the division of the territory between Serbs and Muslims was initiated. The agreement between two nations was verified and adopted at the Municipal Assembly on 13th of April, 1992. Just as the adopted decision on the division of the Vlasenica territory into three municipalities was to be put in practice -- into practice, the Muslim representatives gave up on implementing this decision under pressure from the SDA central leadership. The fear and distrust amongst the population and many people -- the fear and distrust grew among the population and many people, both Serbs and Muslims, left Srebrenica [sic] when the armed conflict began in Bijeljina and Zvornik. Due to the employees -- due to the employees not coming to work because of the uncertain situation and the mass exodus of people, schools and companies were no longer functioning. Representatives were organised to ask the Muslims to return to Vlasenica. However, they did not appear willing to come back. On 21st of April, 1992, the Territorial Defence in Vlasenica was mobilised to prevent property from being looted. No violence was used on this occasion. Serbs who had been expelled by the Muslims in Kladanj, Olovo, and Gorazde started arriving in Vlasenica. Muslims from neighbouring villages also started arriving in the city. They had asked the municipal authorities to provide them with transport to Kladanj and Olovo. The municipal authorities tried to accommodate both Serbian and Muslim requests as far as possible. An issue arose in Vlasenica as the refugees required housing which was not available, so a housing commission was formed to organise temporary accommodation in abandoned Serb and Muslim properties. A reception centre was also created in Susica and buildings belonging to the JNA were used to house refugees and civilians. Permits were issued by the police to allow permanent citizens the ability to move around the area and feel more safe.
