utterances.text: This is a document dated the 23rd of June, 1993, and it's a request by -- by you about the public sale of valuables acquired through the war, and that you as minister of trade are seeking to regulate the sale of war booty, noting that such sales as recently held by Executive Boards of Prijedor and Kotor Varos are -- are of massive proportions and with the implementation of the government conclusion of the 20th of March, 1993, on -- that is on placing state war booty under control you can expect a great influx of -- of objects. So what -- what did you mean by massive proportions? Such sales as recently held by the Executive Boards of Prijedor and Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes. The problem was that there were significant assets left behind in certain local communes and companies. The government of the RS -- or, rather, of the Serbian Republic issued a decree regulating the issue of war booty. It was such property belonging to companies which was found in the territory of Republika Srpska. Some local communes or communities used that property to finance their own needs. Before my arrival at the helm of the ministry of trade, there had been a decree regulating the issue. It was stated that all war booty was to go to the state reserves of the commodity reserves of the RS. It was a separate entity within the ministry of trade. All requests of the commodity reserves to the government went through the ministry that I was heading at that time. Since there were problems and wilful activities in the field that went against that decree, I asked that the government issue their position regarding the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this war booty, isn't this property which is -- which was owned by non-Serbs and which they had to voluntarily, quote/unquote, sign over to the municipal authorities in order to leave?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: If you are familiar with our system as it existed before the war, you know that all companies were public, owned by the state. Physical persons did not have important assets. It was up to the government to deal with property. As for the companies left in those areas, for example, I know that there was -- there was significant quantities of aluminum that was taken out as the JNA units were pulling out and taken to Nevesinje in RS, and that issue had to be regulated. In Sarajevo, too, there were several large depots containing oil and oil derivatives, and that issue, too, fell under the decree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: The government did not deal with personal property.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, I want to move on to the -- to -- in paragraph 38 you said, "I didn't have any contact -- I did not have any occasion to contact Mr. Karadzic until I went into the Republika Srpska government," and that was in August 1995, wasn't it? Mr. Stanic, I need you to be very brief. Did you go into the government in 1995? Were you a member of the -- were you a member of the Assembly in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Not in 1995. I was a member of the Assembly, but I was in the government from the 1st February 1993, and I was an MP from 1995 or even 1996. I'm not sure. As for meeting with President Karadzic, I said that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: -- I had seen him in 1992 at a funeral.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you also -- and you also saw him at the Zvornik meeting on the 30th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: In Zvornik, right. That is true. When I said we didn't meet, I meant we never talked one-on-one about any issues. We did not have any meetings in 1992, and even during my term of office at the Municipal Assembly, President Karadzic never stopped by the Municipal Assembly of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So then what did you mean in the following paragraph where you say, "I know that he would emphasise at every meeting that our soldiers must not be allowed to commit crimes"? Which meetings are you talking about? Are you talking about meetings when you were minister of trade? Why would you be discussing soldiers not being allowed to commit crimes in trade meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about two orders we received in the month of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stanic, if I can --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: One was addressed to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- if I can stop you there. I'm talking about -- you say in your statement: "He would emphasise at every meeting that our soldiers must not be allowed to commit crimes." We just established that.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: I mean this meeting in Zvornik and a series of meetings I had later at the Government of Republika Srpska in the course of 1993 and 1994, and also the orders we received in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in 1993 and 1994, you were minister for trade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Very last point. You were aware of the SDS leadership objective to eradicate the borders with the Serbian states, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: I know it was the objective and the wish of our people to remain part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That was the basic demand of our people, our leadership, our government, and we aspired towards that aim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 24624, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, this is a "Drinski" article, which is the VRS Drina Corps monthly bulletin, dated November 1995, and it's an interview with you. And this is an excerpt within this interview where you're talking about the upcoming elections rather than a retrospective on the war, but you hope that a result of the ongoing negotiations will be a monetary and trade union with Yugoslavia that Serbs will be able to have citizens of RS and FRY. And that Serbs will finally be connected to their mother state. You are now in charge of the customs service of Zvornik, and the policy of the SDS is that the customs borders with FRY will disappear and be moved to the border with the Muslim-Croat federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page of the B/C/S, please, so the witness can see that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall saying that in November 1995, Mr. Stanic, to the "Drinski" bulletin? We can see just above your photograph, the sentence in the second paragraph -- second column, sorry, going down under your photograph, and then also in the top of column 4. Do you recall saying that the policy of the SDS was as I just told you a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: I said our wish and the wish of the people was to stay part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and to have good relations with -- with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Nowadays we have special relationship with Serbia, and you also know that the issue of borders and customs within all of Europe is radically different. There are no borders and customs between 27 states, and there are also tax and customs policies that stand in the way of normal trade. I expected that. I suggested that, and we see it happening. Customs services have less and less work, and we hope that in the period to follow they will be abolished completely. They have been abolished already in the European Union. Why wouldn't they not be abolished between Republika Srpska and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stanic. Your Honours, I have no further questions. And I seek to tender that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The document we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you also tendering the previous document? Public auction or sale of --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, Your Honour. The war booty, that was 24625.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit them all.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P6141 and 6142, respectively, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I've been advised that P06139 now has a translation and can be admitted and I seek for it to be admitted in full. And P06140, the translation has been rectified.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 6139 now has a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We'll do so. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Let me just ask are we free to have translated the rest of this document? Has only the portion that has been translated been admitted into evidence or the whole text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It has been our practice to only admit those portions shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no time now. I can only accept the witness if he accepts the entire interview as his own.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why would I accept it if I haven't read it? I can see the portion that is excerpted, and I agree that it be admitted into evidence. I did advocate the open borders with Yugoslavia, but there may be other portions that do not accurately reflect what I said. I have no time now to read the entire text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then, we won't go any further. Dr. Stanic, you insisted and we it as a leitmotif in documents beginning with page 55 and onwards, that the region of Birac was the Autonomous Region Birac without the prefix Serbian. Was there any other region that was not Serbian Autonomous Region, but only Autonomous Region?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: I believe there were others. I can't remember any specifically now, but I believe there were such districts in other areas. I believe the Semberija region was also called autonomous district, and there was another in Krajina that was not called Serbian, only autonomous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far did you come in organising the organs of authority of the Autonomous Region of Birac? Which authorities were in place to issue executive orders?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Not a single body or agency succeeded in fully assuming its responsibility. It was only our attempt to stop the break-up of Yugoslavia and to show Muslims that we would not accept a unitarian centralised Bosnia-Herzegovina. And when we were establishing these bodies, it was not even our intention to put them into operation because we simply did not have the funds to finance so many bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about Variants A and B. Did anybody from the central authorities send you any queries or controlled in any way whether you adhered to the provisions of documents A and B?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. There was a strong grassroot initiative at the time. There was an empty space. The leadership was in a difficult situation after having to leave Sarajevo, and a lot of initiatives came from the local level. We simply could not expect support or assistance from the central level. We made do consulting with other municipalities and looking at our own particular situation. Every municipality was facing different problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Several things are mentioned here. It is said the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica. What does it mean, Serbian municipality of Vlasenica? What is understood by that term?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: That's a municipality established through joint negotiations between representatives of two peoples. There is a document signed by both parties. It was approved also by representatives of the Muslim people, and it was adopted by an overwhelming majority by the Municipal Assembly. That majority did not mean that only Serbs were meant to live in that area. It implied, of course, that the Muslims living in the area created by these negotiations should remain there or perhaps later decide according to their own wishes to move. There was no mention of ethnically pure municipalities at any point, and I believe there is one of the conclusions that defines this relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When it is said that you were appointed president of the municipality or the president of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica, does it mean that you took over that position in the Muslim municipality of Vlasenica too?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: No. We had serious intentions and goodwill to start implementing that agreement. However, the local representatives of the Muslim people obviously coached by the leadership in Sarajevo and following their instructions abandoned that agreement. We had discussed all these issues in an atmosphere of mutual co-operation, and I believe that agreement had given us a chance to avoid war spreading to Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was in power in Vlasenica throughout 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: In 1991, the authorities were formed by a joint agreement between the SDA and the Serbian majority in the local parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who was in power in the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: I believe the officials who worked in joint authorities continued to work in the Serbian authorities, including myself as president of the joint Assembly and later president of the Assembly of the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have a list of the population here. Which of Vlasenica's municipalities did Cerska belong to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Cerska was --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm just wondering how this arises out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is how the indictment -- actually, the cross-examination today suggests that the Serbs took over power in Vlasenica. However, they continue to be in power, but only in the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica, and here we have a list of settlements in the Muslim municipality of Vlasenica where the Serbs did not take power. The charge of the take-over of power appears in the indictment as one of the gravest charges, even though there was a division of the administration and even though the Muslims who transferred to the Muslim police station is being treated as our dismissal of those Muslims. So what's being suggested is that the Serbs took over power in Vlasenica. What I'm trying to clarify is the -- the circumstances in which there was a changeover of power and did it occur in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow in terms of how it arises from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think Ms. Sutherland dealt with any issue relating to Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. And, Your Honour, if -- if Mr. Karadzic wanted to get this information from the witness, he could have done it in his -- in his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, it was said take-over of power, and what was shown was Exhibit P03214. From page 68 onwards of the transcript we are dealing with the take-over of power by the Serbs, even though it says in all of those documents that it's the government of the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica. So I want to find out from a witness who was in that government what it meant before the war and during the war, what it means, the term "Serbian municipality." When and how did they take over power?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm fine with you putting questions with respect to that decision to take over power, i.e., Exhibit P3214, but you seem to be asking some question about Cerska. So what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stanic, was Cerska an integral part of the municipality of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you take over power in Cerska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Until the end of the war, the area of the old municipality of Vlasenica had a functioning Muslim municipality of Vlasenica. It functioned on a half of the territory. Its headquarters were first located in the Gru [phoen] neighbourhood of Vlasenica. Later it was moved to Cerska itself, and it remained there up until the operations relating to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm just going to read a few things. I'm going to put the question to you. Did you take over power in Cerska, Djurici, Dzemat, Djile, Kerovi [phoen], Gradina, and generally in that half, Puljancici, Macesi, and so on and so forth, Nova Kasaba? At the beginning, did you take over power in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: I said until the end of the war, until operations in Srebrenica, these areas were under the control of the authorities of the Muslim municipality of Vlasenica and by their armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who was in the majority in these neighbourhoods that I have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Of course it was a Muslim-majority population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look -- well, today we saw a series of documents produced on the 19th of April. Same typewriter, same manner. It was a very productive day. Are you able to tell us -- well, you expressed your doubts about these documents. Are you able to tell us who and for what reason would produce these documents that you did not see or sign?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Well, it would definitely be somebody who had reasons to prevent the truth from coming out and from being heard, and that is why I am here, to deny such lies. So far there are been many lies that we have heard in the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I testified there, and now I have the opportunity to state the truth before the International Tribunal. Certain forces which I assume have something to do with corruption and those kind of problems and who are probably in cahoots with the Prosecution are producing these false documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D25422. This is an associated document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you expand a bit more about the reason for making up these false documents? So what's the point of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I can, because today I could understand what the essence is of the intention of the Prosecution. The false document from 1994 signed by Mile Kosoric, an officer of the JNA who only came to Vlasenica at the end of 1993 and who wrote that military detachments were formed under the control of the civilian authorities and the Crisis Staff, this is absolutely not true, and that person could not have known what was going on in Vlasenica at that point in time. And the earlier documents then tie into this document, because on the 21st of April the army entered Vlasenica and the Crisis Staff began to function on the 22nd. It was necessary to show that the civilian authority was the one who organised the army's coming, arrival, and that it was the civilian authorities who were in command of the military forces even though we had an order which we respected in its entirety not to interfere in military operations by the military or by the police, and that is really how it was. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I'll leave it at that. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're on this topic, can we look at D407, please. It's a Defence exhibit, D007. This is the previous document. Well, we can leave this document. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with this document, and can you please look at item 4, and could you please read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm speaking about this document. It was the basis of all of our actions and conduct. Paragraph 4 states: "TO, Territorial Defence, and police forces are under the exclusive command of professional staff, and therefore it is necessary to prevent any interfering in the command of the TO or use of the police forces." That is the instruction coming from the Government of Republika Srpska, dated the 26th of April, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D25422 now. This document was looked at earlier. It's an associated document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stanic, please, could you please look at this document and tell us whether this document is legal. Is there a protocol? Is there a heading, a signature, a stamp?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does have a protocol, a signature, a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is this authentic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what is it that makes this document a legal document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Its preamble.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked about the signature. You said that they were authentic. Is this your signature, and the other one is Djukanovic's?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The documents that we saw that don't have a protocol number or a signature, how would you evaluate their legitimacy?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: It's clear that those are mostly disputable documents that bear a different stamp from this one. This is one element. A number of them does not have my signature, and there is a problem also with the corrected dates. It's true that, in May, all the municipal services, including the economic sector and the financial services sector and the municipal secretariat had stamps like this, and they had all stamps of the Municipal Assembly of Vlasenica, and a number of documents were issued by those services so that we were not in the municipal building in the course of the month of May, so we could not control that process. And that is the reason why probably a whole series of documents was created that we did not have access to, that were not reviewed at the organs of the Municipal Assembly of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you have the Vlasenica Brigade, regardless of what its names were at particular periods of time, and what was your role in supplying that brigade? I'm thinking of the Vlasenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: The Vlasenica Brigade was formed a little bit later. I think that I was already in the Government of Republika Srpska when the Vlasenica Brigade was formed. Earlier I think there was the Vlasenica Battalion which was part of the Sekovici Brigade. The question of supply of the Vlasenica Brigade, primarily food and financing, securing salaries for the army, was mostly entrusted to the Executive Board which we had activated quite early on. That was one of our local initiatives. Some municipalities did not have an active Executive Board, and these activities were carried out by the commissioners' offices and then before that by the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Stanic, the Birac zone, the Vlasenica municipality and the neighbouring municipalities, Nova Kasaba, Vlasenica, Konjevic Polje, and so on, Cerska, at that time were these areas areas where there was combat? Were they theatres of war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is clear that they were combat zones, and sometime from early May 1992, even though there were tensions before that, all the way until 1995, June 1995, these were combat areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you as the president of the municipality, were you also by virtue of your office the president of the council for defence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the time the municipality was founded, from the multi-party elections in 1990 and practically until the 20th of April, when I tried for the last time to convene the National Defence Council. However, the TO commander whom I invited to that meeting, and that was the last time that I spoke with him, he promised to come and he didn't appear, and the other Muslim officials left Vlasenica earlier than that, so that we simply did not have any other officials, Muslim officials, who would be prepared to take part in the work of the Council for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As the president of the Council for National Defence, were you familiar with our obligations towards the civilians. According to international law, did we have any obligations towards them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO STANIC
utterances.text: This was something that was regulated by the federal law for the defence which provided the precise duties in extraordinary conditions, what the duties and authority of this Council for National Defence was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at one more document. This is D1603.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that we -- did you know that -- did you know that we were in contact with the Red Cross and the commissioner for refugees regarding the rights of civilians, the wounded, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm wondering where this is going as a result of cross-examination, but if Mr. Karadzic can be asked not to lead the witness, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it arises from the showing of Exhibit 03240, and it relates to actions towards civilians. Well, I would like to rephrase the question then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the witness denied the existence of the government at the time, but let's continue. Is this your last question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not trying to change the fact that the government did not exist, but let us see what our attitude or position or conduct towards civilians was. Paragraph 7 of this document. Let's first say what meeting this was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, is it possible Mr. Karadzic can lay a foundation question before he --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can Mr. Karadzic lay a foundation question before he gets the document read?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked if Mr. Stanic was familiar with the duties of the warring parties and our duties towards civilians in that zone, regardless of the document but generally, because during the cross-examination the question of the fate of civilians was asked, especially transfers, expulsions, and so on and so forth. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked Dr. Stanic whether this was a combat zone and now you're going to see why.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic's question was: "Well, let us see what our attitude or position or conduct towards civilians was." He's basically just wanting to bring this document up and to show this to the witness. He hasn't laid, in my view, a question -- a foundation question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's conclude your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic. This has been already admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 10 so -- 7 so that we can see day -- the date and then page 10, just so that we can read one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. I told you to stop here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that you said that I could complete my question and complete my examination. But in any event, thank you. Dr. Stanic, thank you for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I thank the Trial Chamber, and I thank the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before we adjourn today, Mr. Tieger, just before the winter recess last year, the Chamber received from the accused his Notice of Special Defence as to count 11, i.e., reprisals, dated 14th of December, 2012. I'm wondering if the Prosecution intends to respond to any procedural or substantive issues arising from that Defence notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We now take on board the fact that any -- that the Chamber would appreciate any potential response within a reasonable time period from this inquiry and we will do so accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, that concludes your evidence. Only behalf of this Trial Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you for making it possible for me to speak the truth before the International Criminal Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
